subject: math
cluster: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems
description: Students use units as a tool to understand and solve multi-step problems. They convert between measurement units using conversion factors (dimensional analysis), track units through a chain of multiplications and divisions to verify that a setup is correct, choose and interpret units consistently when substituting into formulas, and choose and interpret an appropriate scale and origin for the axes of a graph or data display. The unit reasoning, not the arithmetic, is the focus: a correct setup is one whose units cancel to leave exactly the units requested.
subSkills: Build a conversion factor as a fraction equal to $1$ (e.g. $\frac{1\text{ ft}}{12\text{ in}}$) and orient it so the unwanted unit cancels
Chain two or more conversion factors so all intermediate units cancel, leaving the target unit (dimensional analysis)
Convert a rate, including a compound rate such as $\frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$ to $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$, by applying conversion factors to both the numerator and the denominator
Choose units consistently before substituting into a formula and report the answer in the units that formula produces
Use unit analysis to check whether a proposed solution setup is reasonable and to identify the units of an unknown quantity
Choose an appropriate scale (interval per gridline) and origin for an axis given the range of the data
Interpret the scale and origin of a given graph or data display to read off or estimate a value

problemArchetypes.name: Single-factor unit conversion
problemArchetypes.example: Convert $5$ feet to inches. Setup: $5\text{ ft}\times\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}=60\text{ in}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Multi-step (chained) conversion
problemArchetypes.example: Convert $2.5$ miles to feet using $1\text{ mi}=5280\text{ ft}$, then to inches using $1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}$. Setup: $2.5\text{ mi}\times\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}\times\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}=158400\text{ in}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Rate conversion (compound units)
problemArchetypes.example: A car travels at $60\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$. Convert to $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$. Setup: $60\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}\times\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}\times\frac{1\text{ hr}}{3600\text{ s}}=88\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose consistent units for a formula
problemArchetypes.example: Using distance $=$ rate $\times$ time, a runner moves at $8\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$ for $5$ minutes. Convert $5$ min to $300$ s first, then $d=8\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}\times 300\text{ s}=2400\text{ ft}$. Answer: $2400$ ft.

problemArchetypes.name: Interpret units of an unknown (unit reasoning check)
problemArchetypes.example: In the formula $W=Fd$ with force $F$ in newtons (N) and distance $d$ in meters (m), what are the units of $W$? Answer: $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ (joules).

problemArchetypes.name: Choose scale and origin for a graph
problemArchetypes.example: Daily temperatures range from $52^{\circ}\text{F}$ to $89^{\circ}\text{F}$. Choose a reasonable scale and starting value for the vertical axis. Answer: start the axis near $50^{\circ}\text{F}$ (not $0$) and use a scale of $5^{\circ}\text{F}$ per gridline.

problemArchetypes.name: Interpret a given scale/origin to read a value
problemArchetypes.example: A bar graph axis starts at $0$ and each gridline is $250$ units. A bar reaches halfway between the $3$rd and $4$th gridline. What value does it show? Answer: $875$.

problemArchetypes.name: Multi-step word problem combining conversion and a formula
problemArchetypes.example: A water tank fills at $3\ \frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}$. How many gallons does it hold if it fills completely in $2$ hours? Convert $2$ hr to $120$ min, then $3\ \frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\times 120\text{ min}=360\text{ gal}$. Answer: $360$ gal.

Easy.description: Single-step recognition or one conversion factor. Student converts between two directly related units, identifies the correct conversion factor or its orientation, or reads a value off a graph whose scale and origin are stated. One unit conversion, no compound units, no formula.
constraints: Exactly one conversion factor, or a direct read from a labeled axis
Common, familiar conversions (ft/in, ft/yd, min/s, hr/min, m/cm, kg/g, \$ to cents)
Simple (non-compound) units; numbers are small whole numbers or terminate cleanly
Graph items: scale and origin are given; student only reads or names the interval

Medium.description: Two to three steps. Student chains two conversion factors, converts one part of a compound rate, substitutes into a familiar formula after a single conversion, or chooses a reasonable scale/origin for a one-variable data set. Unit cancellation across two factors must be tracked.
constraints: Two chained conversion factors, OR one conversion plus a one-step formula substitution
May involve a compound unit where only the numerator or only the denominator is converted
Numbers may be decimals or require one intermediate rounding stated in the prompt
Graph items: student selects a sensible scale and a nonzero origin from a given data range

Hard.description: Multi-step modeling and reasoning. Student converts a full compound rate (both numerator and denominator), or combines unit conversion with a formula and reports the result in requested units, or reasons about the units of an unknown, or justifies a choice of scale/origin in context. Three or more dependent steps where a wrong unit orientation propagates.
constraints: Compound-rate conversions touching both numerator and denominator (e.g. $\frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}\to\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$)
Combine a multi-factor conversion with substitution into a formula and a final unit check
Require interpreting or deriving the units of an unknown quantity in a formula
Graph items: justify why a chosen origin or scale best displays the data, or interpret a value from a nontrivial scale (e.g. $250$ per gridline, half-gridline reads)

tierSplit.note: This standard uses a single ramped worksheet (Easy early, Hard late). If split into two sheets: tier1 covers Easy to Medium (single and double conversions, reading given graphs); tier2 covers Medium to Hard (compound-rate conversions, conversion-plus-formula problems, unit-of-unknown reasoning, and choosing/justifying scale and origin). No item overlap between tiers.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student inverts the conversion factor, putting the unwanted unit where it cannot cancel
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Converts $5$ ft to inches as $5\times\frac{1}{12}=\frac{5}{12}$ in instead of $5\times 12=60$ in

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student multiplies when they should divide (or vice versa) because they ignore which unit must cancel
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Converts $60$ inches to feet as $60\times 12=720$ ft instead of $60\div 12=5$ ft

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student converts only the numerator of a compound rate and leaves the denominator unconverted
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Converts $60\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$ to $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$ as $60\times 5280=316800\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{hr}}$ but reports it as $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$, never dividing by $3600$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student substitutes into a formula without first making the units consistent
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Computes distance as $8\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}\times 5\text{ min}=40$ ft, using $5$ min directly instead of converting to $300$ s

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats units as if they cannot combine, dropping or mislabeling the units of a product or quotient
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $W=Fd$ with $F$ in N and $d$ in m, reports the units of $W$ as $\frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}}$ or just N instead of $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student insists every graph axis must start at the origin $0$, even when the data is clustered far from zero
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an origin of $0$ with scale $10$ for temperatures from $52^{\circ}$ to $89^{\circ}$, wasting most of the axis, instead of starting near $50^{\circ}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misreads a graph scale, counting gridlines as single units instead of using the stated interval
commonMisconceptions.distractor: On an axis where each gridline is $250$, reads a bar at the $3$rd gridline as $3$ instead of $750$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses the wrong numeric value for a conversion (e.g. confuses feet-per-mile or seconds-per-hour)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Uses $1\text{ mi}=1000\text{ ft}$ or $1\text{ hr}=100\text{ s}$, e.g. converting $60\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$ with $\frac{1\text{ hr}}{60\text{ s}}$ instead of $\frac{1\text{ hr}}{3600\text{ s}}$
